extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers interested in public opinion, journalism, and political communication
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and analyze the factors that shape public opinion and the communication environment (means of communication, social sets, time/attention, language). Useful for scholars, journalists, and students studying how news and social structure influence opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and intensity required to create one public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Probably this is the largest and the most intensive effort to carry quickly a fairly uniform set of ideas to all the people of a nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann details Creel's wartime machinery (Division of News, 6,000 releases; 75,000 Four Minute Men; hundreds of thousands of speeches; posters, lantern slides, periodicals distributed via churches, chambers of commerce, schools). He notes that such scale required dogged work, ingenuity, money and personnel and that nothing like it exists in peace; thus creating a nearly uniform national opinion ordinarily would require extreme measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of communication determine supply and quality of information
rubrics_metrics.description: Travel and trade, the mails, the wires, and radio, railroads, highways, ships, motor cars, and in the coming generation aeroplanes, are, of course, of the utmost influence on the circulation of ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each medium affects both the amount and the character of information; technical, economic and political conditions (e.g., customs inspection, passport formalities, new ports, rates, censorship) modify speed, reach and content of news circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly, cost and supply are barriers to exchange of news and opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The monopolizing of cables ... ports, fuel stations, mountain passes, canals, straits, river courses, terminals, market places means ... a barrier upon the exchange of news and opinion. But monopoly is not the only barrier. Cost and available supply are even greater ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control of physical or infrastructural chokepoints (cables, ports, canals) and prohibitive costs can block or distort information flow even without formal monopoly; policy and economic changes (tariffs, subsidies) alter these barriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Income and community wealth affect access to information
rubrics_metrics.description: The size of a man's income has considerable effect on his access to the world beyond his neighborhood. With money he can overcome almost every tangible obstacle of communication, he can travel, buy books and periodicals...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both individual and community incomes determine how much communication is possible. However, how income is spent is mediated by people's interests and values, so financial capacity interacts with preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-imposed limitations: leisure preferences and lack of curiosity reduce exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: There are portions of the sovereign people who spend most of their spare time and spare money on motoring ... talking always to the same people with minute variations on the same old themes. They cannot really be said to suffer from censorship. They suffer from anemia, from lack of appetite and curiosity for the human scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when material access exists, habits, tastes and social routines lead many to remain isolated in small circles of interest; absence of curiosity is a non-structural but real barrier to information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social set defines admissible information and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: In the social set ... it is finally decided in each phase of a discussion which authorities and which sources of information are admissible, and which not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person's social set (the circle whose approval matters most) shapes what information is attended to, how it is interpreted, and which authorities are trusted; social sets socialize children into canons like Family Tradition, Respectability, Taste and Form that constrain opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social leaders act as custodians and interpreters of social patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Within each social set there are augurs ... who are recognized as the custodians and the interpreters of its social pattern. The social leaders ... must combine an intimate knowledge of the anatomy of their own set with a persistent sense of its place in the hierarchy of sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social leaders determine status signals (invitations, college societies) and monitor other sets; they function as gatekeepers and intermediaries, influencing how standards and opinions flow between groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy and imitation (radiant points of conventionality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of the sets are so placed that they become 'radiant points of conventionality.' Thus the social superior is likely to be imitated by the social inferior ... the powerful, socially superior, successful, rich, urban social set is fundamentally international.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation flows from higher-status groups downward and across communities; international cosmopolitan elites (e.g., London) can set standards whose private affairs become public matters and influence wider opinion, especially in foreign affairs and war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal channels between sets enable circulation of standards
rubrics_metrics.description: There come to be established personal channels from one set to another, through which Tarde's laws of imitation operate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptional individuals who move between sets create conduits for ideas and practices; where such channels are absent, mass publics must rely on mediated accounts and portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited time and attention devoted to public affairs (approx. quarter-hour daily)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three estimates ... agree tolerably well ... over three quarters of those in the selected groups rate rather low the attention they give to printed news of the outer world. ... seventy-one percent ... rate themselves at fifteen minutes a day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey evidence (college students, business/professional men) indicates many people spend around 15 minutes daily on newspapers; this limited attention constrains the amount of news and argument citizens can absorb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper-reading patterns and feature preferences shape information exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Scott asked how many papers they read each day ... 14% read one paper, 46% two, 21% three ... college students named 'the five features which interest you most' (general news, editorials, politics, finance, foreign news ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual preferences (local, political, financial news) and the number of papers read determine which topics are encountered; demographic differences (gender, occupation) affect feature interest and thereby the kind of information people receive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of newspaper space relative to public-affairs interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis ... one hundred and ten newspapers ... averaged ... I. News 55.3% (war 17.9, general 21.8, special 15.6), Illustrations 3.1%, Literature 2.4%, Opinion 7.1%, Advertisements 32.1% ... recomputed (excluding ads) public-affairs-related items totaled about 76.5%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, a large share of editorial space was devoted to public affairs; though proportions change, the net amount may increase even if percentage falls; space allocation affects what readers can learn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words are the chief medium and are compressed/coded, leading to loss of meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The unseen environment is reported to us chiefly by words. ... Telegraphy is expensive ... Press service news is, therefore, usually coded. ... A news item ... translated, coded, and then decoded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coded dispatches, telegraphic abbreviations, and the necessary compression of reports (culling lengthy accounts into short items) prune context and nuance, making precise transmission of complex events difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression of events into brief items telescopes meaning and complicates judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: A correspondent culls an item of print three and a half inches long. The meaning has to be telescoped in such a way as to permit the reader to judge how much weight to give to the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short news items often omit provenance, chains of evidence, and context, forcing readers to infer or imagine much of the background, which can lead to misjudgment or over/underestimation of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language ambiguity and cultural differences produce misinterpretation ('word exchanges')
rubrics_metrics.description: Words, like currency, are tokens of value. ... Some nations constitutionally tend to understate, others to overstate. ... There is a war fluctuation on word exchanges as well as on money exchanges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different linguistic habits and rhetorical conventions across cultures change the effective value of words; translations and cultural registers can inflate or deflate perceived meaning (examples: 'etonnant', 'awful').

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader literacy and comprehension limit the effective transmission of news
rubrics_metrics.description: Millions of those who are watching him can read hardly at all. Millions more can read the words but cannot understand them. Of those who can both read and understand, a good three-quarters ... have some part of half an hour a day to spare for the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when text reaches readers, varying levels of literacy, comprehension, and available time mean only a small fraction can process messages deeply; thus public opinion is often constructed imaginatively from limited cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lucidity of mind (ability to dissociate analogies and appreciate differences) is essential for critical judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to dissociate superficial analogies, attend to differences and appreciate variety is lucidity of mind. ... It is a relative faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical public opinion requires capacity to distinguish crude analogies, attend to specifics, and resist overgeneralization; without such discrimination, opinion is shaped by superficial similarities or sweeping stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized experience increases discrimination and understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: A man who merely rides in other people's automobiles may not rise to finer discrimination ... But let that same man own a car and drive it ... he will describe a difference in carburetors by looking at the rear end of a car a city block away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hands-on involvement and practical experience cultivate finer distinctions and deeper understanding; specialization enhances the ability to perceive relevant differences in complex subjects.
